items.title: Your blood sugar is regulated within a 30% range despite irregular meals
items.claim: Normal fasting blood glucose: 4-6 mmol/L. After a meal: rises to 7-8, then back to baseline within 2 hours. Healthy people maintain this range whether they eat constantly or fast for a day.

options.text: Insulin (from pancreatic beta cells) lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake and storage; glucagon (from alpha cells) raises it by mobilising stored glycogen — a classic antagonistic pair under negative feedback

items.reveal:
After a meal: blood glucose rises. Beta cells in the pancreas detect it via glucokinase and secrete insulin. Insulin tells muscle and fat to take up glucose, and the liver to store it as glycogen.

Between meals: glucose drops. Alpha cells secrete glucagon. Glucagon tells the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose into the blood. If glycogen runs out (after ~24 hours fasting), gluconeogenesis from amino acids and glycerol takes over.

Type 1 diabetes: autoimmune destruction of beta cells. No insulin. Blood glucose unregulated. Discovered to be treatable with injected insulin by Banting and Best (1921, Nobel 1923) — life expectancy of Type 1 patients went from months to decades within a year of insulin's availability.

Type 2 diabetes: insulin RESISTANCE develops in target tissues. Beta cells initially compensate (more insulin) then eventually fail. Affects ~10% of adults globally. Strongly linked to obesity and inactivity.

The brain is unique in burning glucose nearly exclusively (~120 g/day, 20% of total body glucose use) — which is why hypoglycaemia causes confusion, seizures and unconsciousness within minutes.
items.why: Hormones feel like signals from somewhere distant. In glucose regulation, two opposing hormones from the same gland keep blood sugar within a tight band — a textbook example of antagonistic negative feedback.

items.title: Species are vanishing 100 to 1000 times faster than normal
items.claim: The fossil record gives a 'background' extinction rate: roughly 1 species per million per year. Current rates are 100 to 1000 times that — and rising. Many biologists call it the sixth mass extinction.

options.text: Asteroid impact like 66 million years ago
Habitat destruction (especially tropical deforestation), invasive species, climate change, pollution and overharvesting — a multi-cause anthropogenic mass extinction with no single dominant mechanism

items.reveal:
The five previous mass extinctions (Ordovician, Devonian, Permian, Triassic, Cretaceous) each saw 50-95% of species disappear over geological timescales. The Permian was the worst — ~96% of marine species lost over ~60,000 years.

The current rate, calculated from documented vertebrate extinctions (Ceballos, Ehrlich and others), is 100-1000 times background. Insect biomass declines (Hallmann et al. 2017, Krefeld study) show 75% reductions over 27 years in German nature reserves.

Human impacts: forest cover reduced by ~30% globally since 1700; ocean fish biomass down ~50% since 1970; freshwater vertebrates down 84% (WWF Living Planet Report). Climate change adds an accelerating layer.

Protected areas and conservation work — by some measures, extinction rates would have been 4x higher without them.

Mass extinctions reshape evolution for tens of millions of years. We won't return to the world we know within human-relevant timeframes — the species we lose are lost.
items.why: Species loss feels gradual. The rate is geological in magnitude — comparable to events that left fossil-record-defining boundaries. We are living through one.

items.title: You synthesise your body weight in ATP every day
items.claim: ATP is the cell's energy currency. Your body contains only about 50 grams at any moment, but you turn it over so fast that you make and consume the equivalent of your full body mass — 60 to 80 kilograms — daily.
items.prompt: How can a tiny pool turn over so much?

options.text: Each ATP molecule is hydrolysed and re-synthesised hundreds of times per day; mitochondria continuously rebuild ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate using the proton motive force from respiration
Most of the body's mass is ATP
ATP is consumed only during exercise

items.reveal:
An adult at rest uses about 2000 kcal per day. Each ATP hydrolysis releases ~7.3 kcal/mol of free energy under standard conditions, more under cellular conditions.

Working through: ~65 kg of ATP cycled per day, give or take. Each molecule of ATP cycles roughly 1000-1500 times daily.

The cell stores essentially no ATP for emergencies. It maintains a flux instead. Stop respiration and your ATP pool depletes in seconds — which is exactly why cyanide is so fast.

Muscles store some quick-access energy as phosphocreatine (a few seconds of all-out sprint) and glycogen (~minutes), but ATP itself is continuously regenerated, not stockpiled.

This is metabolism's deep design choice: a small, dynamic currency pool, refilled by continuous oxidation of food.
items.why: Energy storage feels like the obvious solution. Cells went the other way — keep almost no ATP, rebuild it constantly. The flux IS the metabolism.
